beats.say: Aaker's model says brand equity comes from five assets: awareness, perceived quality, associations, loyalty, and other proprietary assets like trademarks.
Two backpacks. One has more pockets and a better warranty. The other is Louis Vuitton, and it sells for many times the price.
That premium is equity at work. People know it, rate it, link it with luxury and stay loyal.
Use it like this: score the brand on all five, then build up the weakest one first.

m-agency-false-economy-bots.title: The agency false economy, three types of bots and three skill clusters
m-agency-false-economy-bots.speaker: Geoff Clarke, IPG Mediabrands Australia, Week 11

beats.say: Upstream work is now mostly AI driven, but downstream work is still manual. That's a false economy. The fix: trigger bots, automatic bots and schedule bots, freeing people for new skills.
Picture the team buried in TV bookings and reconciliations, slogging through it all by hand.
Then the bots take over. An email lands, a trigger bot starts, an automatic bot acts, a schedule bot runs overnight. About two hundred and seven thousand hours saved.
Use it like this: find the manual work, pick the bot, and move people into data, creative and strategic thinking.
The Ansoff matrix maps four ways to grow. Penetration sells more to the same market. Market development finds new markets, product development makes new products, and diversification does both.
Picture Allen's lollies. Penetration means more of the lolly aisle. Selling nostalgia to adults is market development. Intense flavours for Gen Z is product development.
Drinks would be diversification, the riskiest corner. So test it cheaply first, with a collaboration.
Use it like this: put an option in each box, weigh the risk against the brand's strengths, and recommend one.
The BCG matrix sorts a company's brands by market growth and market share. Stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs. Each one needs a different budget.
KitKat is a cash cow: a huge share of a mature chocolate market, throwing off money. A new Gen Z lolly range is a question mark: a growing market, but a tiny share.
A fading niche line is a dog. So milk the cash cow to fund the stars and best question marks, and prune the dogs.
Use it like this: place each brand on the grid with evidence, then show where the budget should flow.

m-brand-definition-five-reasons.title: Papps' brand definition and the five reasons brands matter
m-brand-definition-five-reasons.speaker: Justin Papps, Tenet, Week 3

beats.say: A brand is the beliefs that predispose people to choose you. It matters for five reasons: economic engine, behavioural shortcut, strategy in action, culture shaper, and volatility moat.
Take two backpacks. Louis Vuitton costs about fifteen times more, with fewer compartments and a worse warranty. People still pay. That's the brand.
Brands mean margin. An iPhone sells for over three times what it costs to make, a margin above sixty-seven percent.
Use it like this: argue brand as a commercial asset. Attention is cheap, memory is expensive, preference is priceless.

m-brand-eye-level.title: Brand eye level (and the value exchange)
m-brand-eye-level.speaker: Bryce Coombe, Hypetap, Week 10

beats.say: Brand eye level asks what role you play in people's lives. Leadership means experts. Eye to eye means relatable creators. Subservient means making life easier. And the value exchange is the product in real life.
Kmart signed two TV celebrities. Good on paper, but viewers said, these two don't shop at Kmart.
A recipe creator cooking with the product in real life beat strict brand scripts on sentiment, and cost less.
Use it like this: set the eye level first, then give creators freedom to show the product.

m-brand-on-one-page.title: The brand on one page (purpose, positioning, platform, personality)
m-brand-on-one-page.speaker: Brent Smart, B.Smart, Week 4

beats.say: The brand on one page: purpose, positioning, creative platform, and personality written as tensions. Four short lines every team can work from.
Telstra's page. Purpose: a connected future for everyone. Positioning: engineering possibility. Platform: wherever we go.
Personality: ambitious in ideas, humble in voice. So the ads were handmade stop-motion, and viewers read that craft as care.
Use it like this: write all four lines for the brand, then show how craft and consistency bring them to life.

m-brand-stretch.title: Five brand stretch considerations (stretch map and McKinsey matrix)
m-brand-stretch.speaker: Shannon Wright, Nestle Oceania, Week 5

beats.say: Before stretching a brand, check five things. Positioning fit, distance from the core, consumer permission, risk versus reward, then test and monitor.
Heinz soup is a near step. Pasta sauce, a credible stretch. Vodka? Shoppers squint. It only worked thanks to the vodka pasta moment.
Allen's tested its stretch cheaply, with Pepsi and Mountain Dew collaborations instead of building new products alone.
So walk every extension through all five checks, then launch, collaborate or avoid.

m-brief-to-real-problem.title: The brief, the expected response, the real problem, the solution
m-brief-to-real-problem.speaker: Brendan Willenberg, Executive Creative Director, Week 9

beats.say: Creativity is fancy problem solving. Start with the brief, then the expected response. Dig for the real problem underneath, and only then build the solution.
Extra's brief: sell more gum. The expected response? A bigger ad.
But the real problem? At the checkout, everyone's on their phone and never notices the gum. So the Bad Breath Index put gum into the checkout itself.
Use it like this: brief the problem, not what you want to say.

m-category-entry-points.title: Category entry points (CEPs)
m-category-entry-points.speaker: Jenni Romaniuk, Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, Better Brand Health, 2022

beats.say: Category entry points are the cues that send people into a category: occasions, needs, places and people. The more of them a brand links to, the more often it comes to mind.
Three people want a snack. One is studying late, one is on a road trip, one just needs a break. KitKat owns the break.
To grow, KitKat can link itself to new entry points, like after study or a road trip. Each new link is another moment it comes to mind.
Use it like this: list the category's entry points, see which ones rivals own, and claim an under-used one.

m-consistency-not-sameness.title: Consistency, not sameness
m-consistency-not-sameness.speaker: Shannon Wright, Week 5; Brent Smart, Week 4; Libby Hogson, Week 6; Nicky Barton, Week 12

beats.say: Consistency, not sameness. Keep the core idea, voice and assets. Update the executions, tension and channels. And never let a bored brand manager change everything.
KitKat still says have a break. But Gen Z can't switch off, so the break is now for the mind, not just the body.
Meanwhile a new manager, bored of the old ads, wants to scrap it all. That throws away years of built memory.
Use it like this: turn up differently each time, but keep the idea, voice and craft the same.

m-creative-brief.title: The creative brief (Kraft Easy Mac)
m-creative-brief.speaker: Andrew Baxter, Australian Pork Limited, Week 8

beats.say: The creative brief is a set of questions, answered in order. What's the problem? Who's the audience, and what's the insight? What's different? What's the one thing to say? And why should anyone believe it?
Take Kraft's Easy Mac. The brief targets mums, for teenage boys who get home starving. The one thing to say: it fills them up, fast.
The line was kill hunger fast. The client balked at the word kill, so it became the hunger blaster.
Use it like this: one line per answer, ending in one message and one reason to believe, both tied to the insight.

m-creativity-is-measurable.title: Creativity is measurable (if it's not bold, it's dumb)
m-creativity-is-measurable.speaker: Brent Smart, Week 4; Brendan Willenberg, Week 9

beats.say: Creativity is measurable. Creative ads deliver about two and a half times the revenue growth and four times the profit. Dull work costs millions extra, and earned media is the real prize.
In the meeting, the safe idea gets nods. The bold idea makes everyone squirm. If it's not bold, it's dumb.
Yellow Pages' treehouse used zero paid media. NRMA's koalas went from thirty-sixth to fifth strongest brand. Bold paid off.
Use it like this: back bold work with the numbers, because the biggest risk is taking no risk.

m-current-vs-future-demand.title: Current demand vs future demand (15/85)
m-current-vs-future-demand.speaker: Brent Smart, B.Smart (formerly Telstra and IAG), Week 4

beats.say: Current versus future demand. Only about fifteen percent of buyers are in market right now. The other eighty-five percent are future buyers.
Don't just talk to the four hands that are up right now. That student buying a phone in three years is worth reaching today.
So Telstra swapped dry, rational offers for emotional brand building, so people would remember it when their contract ran out.
Use it like this: split your plan into converting today's buyers and building memories for tomorrow's.
Diffusion of innovations says new products spread through five groups: innovators, early adopters, the early majority, the late majority and laggards.
A new app lands. Innovators grab it for the novelty. Early adopters show it off. The majority waits for proof, and laggards join only when they have to.
To win the majority, make it easy to try and easy to see other people using it.
Use it like this: find the group you have now, aim the message at the next one, and make trying it easy.

m-distinctive-brand-assets.title: Distinctive brand assets (and the DBA paradox)
m-distinctive-brand-assets.speaker: Justin Papps, Week 3; Brent Smart, Week 4; Shannon Wright, Week 5; research from Ipsos and SYSTEM1, building on Jenni Romaniuk

beats.say: Distinctive brand assets trigger your brand in memory: visuals like logo and colour, sounds, characters, and words like slogans. Oddly, the most used are often the least effective.
The ad just says, have a... and the whole family finishes it: a break! The asset does the work.
Telstra had no colour it could own, so it built handmade stop-motion animals instead. Before spending, audit which assets people actually recognise.
Use it like this: audit your assets, keep the ones that work, and repeat them until they're yours.

m-dont-add-channels.title: If you can't add budget, don't add channels
m-dont-add-channels.speaker: Nicky Barton, Mutinex, Week 12

beats.say: If you can't add budget, don't add channels. Across eighty-three brands, keeping the same channels with more budget grew about four percent. More channels with more budget, about two. More channels on a cut fell nearly seven, and a big cut, about eight.
A retailer facing a budget cut wants TikTok, podcasts and billboards all at once. Spread that thin, and every channel goes quiet.
Better to keep your strongest two or three channels at full weight, protect long-lasting TV, and stay on air. Going dark costs you later.
Use it like this: concentrate spend, protect brand channels, and stay consistent.

m-double-jeopardy.title: Double jeopardy law
m-double-jeopardy.speaker: Andrew Ehrenberg; popularised by Byron Sharp, How Brands Grow, 2010

beats.say: Double jeopardy says small brands suffer twice. They have fewer buyers, and those buyers are slightly less loyal. So growth comes from penetration.
Watch the cola fridge. Coke buyers stream past. Pepsi gets fewer of them, and even its own buyers often grab a Coke.
So a Pepsi loyalty app hits a ceiling. The answer is broad reach and wider availability, to recruit light buyers.
Use it like this: when a plan bets on loyalty, argue for reach instead. Loyalty follows share.

m-earned-media.title: Earned media as brand building
m-earned-media.speaker: Libby Hogson, Week 6; Brent Smart, Week 4; Brendan Willenberg, Week 9

beats.say: Earned media is coverage you earn, not buy. It needs ambassadors matched to the moment, credible people and content, real news relevance, and clear measures.
A family watches the evening news. A charity worker on the ground explains the crisis. Nobody paid for that slot, so they trust it more than an ad.
Rexona couldn't afford cluttered sport sponsorship, so it made Pitvertising and got everyone talking. If you can't buy media, earn it.
UNICEF Australia's news mentions rose two hundred and seventy percent. So find a genuine story and the right voice, then track your share of voice.

m-effective-advertising.title: What the most effective advertising is (famous, emotional, single-minded, memorable)
m-effective-advertising.speaker: Andrew Baxter, Australian Pork Limited, Week 8; drawing on UK effectiveness research

beats.say: The most effective advertising is famous, emotional, single-minded and memorable. And differentiation is the biggest brand driver of all.
Share a Coke put names on the bottles. People hunted for their own name and shared the photos. Famous, and personal.
Why emotion? Around ninety-five percent of buying is intuitive, so feelings beat facts.
Use it as a checklist: score the campaign on each trait, and fix the weakest one first.

m-excess-share-of-voice.title: Excess share of voice (ESOV)
m-excess-share-of-voice.speaker: John Philip Jones, 1990; extended by Les Binet and Peter Field

beats.say: Excess share of voice compares your slice of category advertising with your share of market. Voice minus market is the excess.

steps.text: **Share of voice** your slice of ads
**Share of market** your slice of sales

beats.say: Brands that shout louder than their size tend to grow. Every ten points of excess is worth roughly half to one point of market share a year.

board.title: The **rule of thumb**
board.caption: about **0.5 to 1** share point a year

beats.say: UNICEF Australia lifted its broadcast share of voice from twenty to fifty-five percent, far above its share of donations, and awareness rose.
Use it like this: compare share of voice with share of market, set the gap to fit your growth goal, and make the work creative.

m-fame-uniqueness-grid.title: Fame vs uniqueness grid (distinctive asset audit)
m-fame-uniqueness-grid.speaker: Shannon Wright, Nestle Oceania, Week 5; the grid comes from Jenni Romaniuk's distinctive asset research

beats.say: The fame versus uniqueness grid audits your brand assets. Each one lands in a box: use or lose, avoid solo use, invest potential, or ignore.
A shopper hears just Have a break, and instantly thinks KitKat. Famous and unique. Use it or lose it.
But a plain blue bank billboard? People guess three different banks. Famous, but shared by rivals. Invest potential at best.
So list every asset, place each one on the grid, then protect it, build it, or drop it.
Before writing a brief, scan the five Cs: company, culture, category, connections and consumer.
Say the brief is a low-sugar sports drink. The company has a new line. And culture? Run clubs are booming.
Gatorade and Powerade own the category. Runners live on Strava and TikTok. And the consumer? Someone who just finished a race.
So pull one implication from each C, then boil them down to a single insight for the brief.

m-four-creative-principles.title: Four creative principles (Rexona, Extra, Kia, V Energy)
m-four-creative-principles.speaker: Brendan Willenberg, Executive Creative Director, Week 9

beats.say: Four creative principles, each matched to a problem. Constraint sparks ideas. A new idea in a familiar context breaks habits. Lean into the uncomfortable truth. And call out the category.
Rexona had a tiny budget, so it earned media with Pitvertising. Kia's hybrid had nothing new, so it said nothing, brilliantly.
V Energy couldn't beat Red Bull at its own game. So it called out the whole category, and said one thing over and over.
Use it like this: name the shape of the problem, then pick the matching principle.

m-four-pillars-brand-strategy.title: The four pillars of brand strategy
m-four-pillars-brand-strategy.speaker: Justin Papps, Tenet, Week 3

beats.say: Four pillars hold up a brand strategy: relevance, distinctiveness, consistency and availability. Land all four and you get cut-through.
McDonald's ticks every box. It meets a real need, the golden arches stand out, and they've barely changed in decades.
And it's available two ways. It comes to mind when you're hungry, and there's one on every corner.
Use it like this: score your brand on each pillar, then fix the weakest one first.

m-four-principles-cultural-relevance.title: Four principles for brand conversations (cultural relevance)
m-four-principles-cultural-relevance.speaker: Shannon Wright, Nestle Oceania, Week 5

beats.say: To join culture, follow four principles. Meet people where they are, nail tone and timing, know the brand's role, and subvert your own equity.
People argued online about how to eat a KitKat. Snap the fingers, or bite straight in? Twenty-seven million engagements.
A debate about your brand is a jackpot. KitKat fanned the flames instead of settling it.
So only join a conversation when the brand has a real reason to be there, with the right tone at the right moment.

m-four-ps.title: The 4Ps (marketing mix)
m-four-ps.speaker: Andrew Baxter, Australian Pork Limited, Week 8; from E. Jerome McCarthy

beats.say: The four Ps are the levers you control: product, price, place and promotion. Baxter says they haven't changed, only how we execute.
Raise the price, then run constant discounts, and shoppers learn to wait for the sale. It stops feeling premium.
Nike pulled back from retailers. Fewer shelves meant fewer people saw it, so place hurt promotion too.
So link every P to the same target and positioning, and the whole mix sends one signal.
Get, who, to, by squeezes a brief into one sentence. Get the audience, who face a problem, to change something, by one proposition.
Picture business travellers who switched to a rival airline on price. Qantas wants them back.
So the brief reads: get lapsed business travellers, who chose on price, to choose Qantas again, by reminding them every flight comes home.
So fill all four slots, and keep the by single-minded.
The golden circle has three rings. Why is your purpose. How is the distinctive way you deliver it. What is the stuff you sell.
Most companies start outside in: here's our computer, it's fast. Apple starts with why: we challenge the status quo, and we happen to make computers.
People buy into beliefs. But the why must be genuine and backed by proof, or it's just empty words.
Use it like this: write the brand's why, how and what in one line each, then check the why has proof.

lines.text: **Why, how, what** in a line each

m-influencer-risk-compliance.title: Influencer risk and compliance (disclosure, AIMCO, brand safety)
m-influencer-risk-compliance.speaker: Bryce Coombe, Hypetap, Week 10

beats.say: With influencers, the brand carries the legal risk, not the creator. A free product counts as paid advertising, so disclose it. Know the risk types, follow the industry code, and check brand safety properly.
One washing powder brand signed a creator without checking her other content, and left the comments open. The brand, not the creator, wore it.
Never trust a screen grab. Check deleted posts, fit, swearing and politics before you sign.
Use it like this: disclose, vet, contract and measure, and name the risk each one cuts.

m-jobs-to-be-done.title: Jobs to be done
m-jobs-to-be-done.speaker: Clayton Christensen, Harvard Business School, Competing Against Luck, 2016

beats.say: Jobs to be done says people hire products to make progress in a circumstance. Every job has a functional, an emotional and a social side.

steps.text: **Social** how they want to be seen

beats.say: Early morning commuters were buying thick milkshakes. Not for the taste. A shake made a long, boring drive interesting, and kept them full until lunch.
So the real competitors were bananas, bagels and boredom, not other milkshakes.
Use it like this: write the job in one sentence, name the surprising rivals, and do that job better.
Keller's brand equity pyramid builds a brand in four steps. Salience first, then meaning, then response, and finally resonance at the top.
Salience asks: do shoppers think of you when they buy? Meaning is what you do and stand for. Response is what they think and feel about it.
Resonance is the peak: loyal fans who feel they belong, like Apple fans queueing for a launch.
Use it like this: find the level where the brand is stuck, then plan activity to lift it one step up.

m-kings-planning-cycle.title: Stephen King's planning cycle and four rules of planning
m-kings-planning-cycle.speaker: Tim Collier, Cummins & Partners, Week 7; from Stephen King's JWT Planning Guide (1974)

beats.say: Stephen King's planning cycle asks five questions. Where are we? Why are we there? Where could we be? How could we get there? Are we getting there?
Telstra started as a national punchline, barely above the tax office. Why? Boring, transactional ads.
Where could it be? A loved brand. How? Emotional, crafted brand building. Then track brand health, and the loop starts again.
So walk the brand through every stage honestly. Evaluation is never the end, it's the next starting point.
Last touch attribution gives the final click all the credit for a sale. So budgets drift to the bottom of the funnel, the brand starves, and privacy rules are breaking the tracking anyway.
It's like a group assignment where whoever hits submit gets the whole mark.
Nike moved spend to the bottom of the funnel. People stopped seeing its ads, and the brand faded from memory.
Use it like this: credit the ads people saw but never clicked, and measure the whole market.

m-lateral-thinking.title: Lateral thinking and how ideas happen
m-lateral-thinking.speaker: Brendan Willenberg, Executive Creative Director, Week 9; from Edward de Bono

beats.say: Lateral thinking, from Edward de Bono. Vertical thinking moves logically with the pieces you have. Lateral thinking changes the pieces by questioning the assumption. Ideas are new combinations, and AI should be an antagonist.
Extra gum joined two things: gum and the checkout scanner. The Bad Breath Index nudged shoppers right at the till.
Rexona joined a logo with an armpit: Pitvertising. No new inputs, just a new connection.
Use it like this: write the obvious answer, then reframe the problem so competitors can't copy you.

m-leaky-bucket.title: The leaky bucket
m-leaky-bucket.speaker: Shannon Wright, Nestle Oceania, Week 5 (on Allen's)

beats.say: The leaky bucket says brand health drains. The bucket holds today's buyers. Natural loss and trend pressure leak them out. A refill means new buyers.
Allen's lollies look healthy today. But older fans drift away, and health trends pull younger ones off too.
So Allen's refills the bucket. A playground, not a museum: intense flavours and wild textures for Gen Z.
Even a strong brand has to keep recruiting new buyers, or it slowly runs dry.

m-long-and-short-60-40.title: The long and the short of it (60/40 brand vs activation)
m-long-and-short-60-40.speaker: Brent Smart, Week 4; Nicky Barton, Week 12; from Les Binet and Peter Field

beats.say: The long and the short of it. Brand building is long-term and emotional, lifting your base. Activation is short-term and rational, spiking sales. The benchmark is about sixty forty.

board.title: The long and **the short** of it

beats.say: Brent Smart found Telstra at just twenty percent brand. He didn't leap to sixty. His first move was fifty fifty.
Here's why. A sale cuts the price and shoppers rush in, then vanish when it ends. Brand building keeps people coming back.
Use it like this: plan both speeds, aim for sixty forty, and agree brand health measures before year one.

m-magnet-not-mirror.title: A magnet, not a mirror (the mirror test)
m-magnet-not-mirror.speaker: Brent Smart, B.Smart, Week 4

beats.say: A magnet, not a mirror. Most ads mirror the category and look like everyone else. A magnet is distinctive enough to pull people in.
On the TV, three ads in a row: real people being real people. The family can't tell which brand is which.
That's the mirror test. Take a still, remove the logo, and put it beside three rivals. If nobody can pick yours, it's a mirror.
Use it like this: run the test on the brand's ads, then pitch a distinctive direction tied to its positioning.

m-marketing-funnel.title: The marketing funnel (with reach and frequency)
m-marketing-funnel.speaker: Andrew Baxter, Week 8; Libby Hogson, Week 6; Nicky Barton, Week 12

beats.say: The marketing funnel moves buyers from awareness and knowledge, to liking and preference, to conviction and purchase.
A shopper notices a new juice on the big screen. Next visit, she prefers it to the others. Then she grabs one and buys.
Baxter's media rule: reach about sixty-five percent of the audience at least three times. One exposure isn't enough.

board.title: Reach and **frequency**
board.caption: of the audience, **three times** or more

beats.say: UNICEF spent ninety-five percent at the bottom and starved the top. So set an objective for every stage, and keep the top full.

m-marketing-mix-modelling.title: Marketing mix modelling (MMM) and probabilistic thinking
m-marketing-mix-modelling.speaker: Nicky Barton, Mutinex, Week 12

beats.say: Marketing mix modelling feeds in years of weekly sales, spend, price, seasonality, the economy and competitors. Out comes what drove sales, the return by channel, and where the next dollar goes. It's Bayesian, and privacy safe.
Think of predicting who'll watch the next episode. You start with what you know about viewers, then update as evidence comes in.
No individual is tracked. It reads the whole market, so it looks less precise, but it's more honest.
Use it like this: explain the inputs and outputs, then move the next dollar where it works hardest.
Views, likes and engagement explain attention. Growth is different: visibility, mental availability, share of voice, perception and behaviour change.
A recipe campaign gets a million likes, and the team cheers. But do more people name the brand unprompted?
Growth looks like this: shoppers talking about your brand, not a rival's, then searching for it and buying it.
Use it like this: report attention, but judge success on growth, compared apples with apples.

m-media-logic-flow.title: The logic flow in media decision-making (and eight channel inputs)
m-media-logic-flow.speaker: Ali Coysh, Initiative, Week 11

beats.say: Media decisions follow a logic flow. Start with the journey stage. Find the bond or barrier. Set the media role. Then narrow down channel, platform and environment, guided by eight inputs.
NRMA Insurance in Queensland had a barrier: locals saw it as an outsider. So media's role was building local credibility.
The environment was The Courier Mail. A Help Our Highway partnership pushed to fix the Bruce Highway, and the government committed four hundred and sixty-seven million dollars.
Use it like this: name the barrier first, make the media role answer it, then pick the place.

m-media-then-vs-now.title: Then vs now: the role of media (paid, owned, earned, shared)
m-media-then-vs-now.speaker: Ali Coysh, Initiative, Week 11

beats.say: Media used to plan, buy and report on paid space. Now it orchestrates whole experiences across owned, earned, shared and paid. That's the shift.
Why the change? More channels, more specialists, tighter budgets, and a data boom under privacy laws. Creative and media agencies now compete for strategy.
NRMA's highway campaign did all four: a paid news partnership, earned coverage, shared talk, and its own channels.
Use it like this: plan all four connections together, not paid media alone.

m-mental-and-physical-availability.title: Mental and physical availability
m-mental-and-physical-availability.speaker: Justin Papps, Week 3; Brent Smart, Week 4; Libby Hogson, Week 6; Bryce Coombe, Week 10; Nicky Barton, Week 12; from Byron Sharp, How Brands Grow

beats.say: Brands grow by being easy to think of and easy to buy. That's mental and physical availability, built through reach and distinctive assets.
A shopper wants a snack. Crumb and Co pops into her head, and it's right there on the shelf. Sale made.
Now the opposite. Nike pulled back from stores and chased only the last click. Fewer people saw it, and awareness faded.
Use it like this: check both. Will buyers think of you, and can they find you easily?

m-mmm-five-analogies.title: How the model thinks: five analogies (baseline, adstock, diminishing returns)
m-mmm-five-analogies.speaker: Nicky Barton, Mutinex, Week 12

beats.say: Five analogies for how the model thinks. A cafe on a busy corner. A song stuck in your head. The fifth slice of pizza. Last year's star. And a flight simulator.
The corner cafe sells coffee with no ads at all: that's baseline. Ads that keep working after they stop are adstock, like Slip, Slop, Slap.
Each extra dollar adds less, like a fifth slice of pizza. A channel's average can hide what the next dollar does. So test the plan first.
Use it like this: strip out baseline, credit carry-over, find saturation, and test before committing budget.

m-motivators-discriminators.title: King's motivators and discriminators (and the three appeals)
m-motivators-discriminators.speaker: Stephen King's JWT Planning Guide (1974), included in the Week 7 notes via Tim Collier

beats.say: Stephen King split brand appeal in two. Motivators are category must-haves. Discriminators set one brand apart. Both draw on the senses, reason and emotions.
In the laundry aisle, every detergent gets clothes clean. That's a motivator. Without it, you're not even on the list.
But one smells of fresh linen and has a friendly mascot. That discriminator wins her over, with no price war.
So meet the motivators, then build a discriminator, ideally emotional, so you never compete on price alone.

m-pestle.title: PESTLE analysis
m-pestle.speaker: Francis Aguilar's environmental scanning, 1967; later PEST and PESTLE

beats.say: PESTLE scans the big forces around a market. Political and economic. Social and technological. Legal and environmental. Six forces no single brand controls.
Take an Australian beer brand. Younger people are drinking less. Social media is now their search engine. Ad rules are strict, and the cost of living bites.
So the response writes itself: a premium no-alcohol range, sold through creators, inside the ad rules.
Use it like this: pick the two or three forces that matter most, give a real example of each, and say what the brand should do.

lines.text: Pick the **two or three** that matter

beats.say: Porter's five forces explain why some industries make more money than others. Rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, the power of buyers and the power of suppliers. Strong forces squeeze margins.
Bottled water feels all five. Rivals everywhere, anyone can launch one, and tap water is free. So most brands fight on price.
Then Liquid Death built a brand nobody could copy. Buyers happily paid more, and rivals were locked out.
Use it like this: rate each force high, medium or low, find the strongest, and show how the brand can weaken it.

m-prompted-unprompted-awareness.title: Prompted vs unprompted (top-of-mind) awareness and the measurement chain
m-prompted-unprompted-awareness.speaker: Libby Hogson, UNICEF Australia, Week 6

beats.say: Awareness comes in levels. Prompted, you recognise the name. Unprompted, you name it unaided. Top of mind, it comes out first.
A researcher asks, name a children's charity. One person shrugs. The other says UNICEF straight away. That's top of mind.
Top-of-mind people had nineteen percent donation intent. Prompted only? Just seven. Nearly triple.
So track the whole chain, from ad awareness, to unprompted awareness, to intent, and finally to market share.
Research-led positioning has four steps. Plot the facts, write the positioning, back it with proof points, then repeat a single message.
UNICEF's research found most people didn't know it was a hundred percent donor funded. Hearing that lifted opinion. Little known, big lift: back that fact.
So the proof points went on air: there in over a hundred and ninety countries, help within forty-eight hours. One message: Always there.
So research, position, prove, then say one thing again and again.

m-right-message-four-steps.title: Right message, right person, right place, right time (strategy, idea, make it, place it)
m-right-message-four-steps.speaker: Andrew Baxter, Australian Pork Limited, Week 8

beats.say: Advertising is four rights: the right message, to the right person, in the right place, at the right time.
At three in the afternoon, the fast food screen shows snacks, and a passing tradie stops.
By six, it switches to family meals, and a mum with her kids heads straight in.
Behind every ad sit four steps: strategy, idea, make it, place it. And always go where the eyeballs are, which today means the phone.

m-seven-ps.title: The 7Ps (extended marketing mix)
m-seven-ps.speaker: Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner, 1981

beats.say: The seven Ps take the classic four, product, price, place and promotion, and add three for services: people, process and physical evidence.
Qantas promises the Spirit of Australia. Friendly crew are the people. Smooth check-in is the process. Lounges and uniforms are the physical evidence.
But if the app is clunky and flights run late, no advertising can hold that promise up.
Use it like this: for a service brand cover all seven, but spend most time on the three that prove the promise.

lines.text: Focus on the **three** that prove it

m-single-minded-proposition.title: The single-minded proposition (one message)
m-single-minded-proposition.speaker: Tim Collier, Week 7; Andrew Baxter, Week 8; Libby Hogson, Week 6; Brendan Willenberg, Week 9

beats.say: The single-minded proposition is the one idea your ad must say. Just one, an invitation not a claim, repeated in new ways.
In the meeting, the client wants to say everything: cheaper, faster, greener, tastier. The creative's eyes glaze over.
Baxter's rule: fifteen words or fewer, and the best billboards use six. Powerful wash in cold water. Instantly clear.
So cut every message down to one, make it an invitation, and repeat it until it's yours.

m-stp.title: Segmentation, targeting and positioning (STP)
m-stp.speaker: Justin Papps, Week 3; Estelle Gohil, Week 2

beats.say: Segmentation, targeting and positioning. Split the market into groups, choose which ones to serve, then own a distinct place in their minds.
Picture the plaza. Students want cheap and quick, parents want healthy, and seniors want a chat. Each group is a segment.
Targeting means choosing, with trade-offs. Apple picked people who value premium tech and simplicity, and positioned itself on unlocking their creativity.
Use it like this: for any brand, name the segment you'd target, why, and the single position you'd own.

m-swot.title: SWOT analysis
m-swot.speaker: Albert Humphrey and colleagues, Stanford Research Institute, 1960s

beats.say: SWOT analysis audits a brand's situation before you set strategy. Strengths and weaknesses are internal, things you control. Opportunities and threats are external, out in the market.
Take Telstra. Strength: the biggest network. Weakness: a reputation barely above the tax office. Opportunity: the Olympics. Threat: cheaper rivals winning on price.
The value is in the links. Use the network strength to seize the Olympics, and fix the dull ads before rivals exploit them.
Use it like this: two or three specific, evidenced points per box, then the strategic moves they point to.

lines.text: Two or three **specific** points per box

m-system-1-system-2.title: System 1 and System 2 thinking
m-system-1-system-2.speaker: Justin Papps, Week 3; Andrew Baxter, Week 8; Estelle Gohil, Week 2; from Daniel Kahneman

beats.say: System one is fast and intuitive, about ninety-five percent of our thinking. System two is slow and logical, only five percent. Brands work as mental shortcuts.
In the drinks aisle, nobody weighs every can on sugar and price. System one just reaches for the familiar red one.
That's why emotional advertising works best. People buy on intuition, then post-rationalise with the facts.
Use it like this: aim brand building at system one, with familiar, distinctive cues that make choosing effortless.

m-three-reasons-influencer.title: Peer validation, algorithmic trust and cultural resonance
m-three-reasons-influencer.speaker: Bryce Coombe, Hypetap, Week 10

beats.say: Influencer isn't just another interruptive channel, for three reasons. Peer validation, algorithmic trust, and cultural resonance, worth about two hundred and forty-six percent more than standard attention.
A creator reviews a serum. A viewer thinks, she's just like me. Then she searches it on TikTok, Google, even an AI assistant, and finds what creators said. Social is now search.
Use it like this: pick the reason that serves your goal, and justify the spend with it.
A strong position lines up three truths: a brand belief, an audience truth and a product truth, all saying the same thing.

steps.text: **Product truth**: a fact that proves it

beats.say: Take KitKat. At three o'clock an office worker feels the drag. Everyone needs a break. That's the audience truth.
And the bar is made to be broken, two fingers that snap apart. The product proves the belief: breaks are good.
Have a break, have a KitKat says all three at once. So find each truth, and fix whichever one is missing.

m-three-ways-research-drives-growth.title: Three ways market research drives growth
m-three-ways-research-drives-growth.speaker: Estelle Gohil, Fiftyfive5, Week 2

beats.say: Market research drives growth in three ways. First, identify where to play. Then execute how to win. Finally, evaluate performance with the metrics that matter.
A university asks where to play. Demand data maps every course on attractiveness and performance, showing which programs to grow.
But numbers can't say why students choose. So qualitative research guides how to win, shaping the offer, the positioning and the creative.
Then track customer experience, brand and sentiment. Use it like this: for any brand, name the research at each stage and the decision it unlocks.

m-ubersight-trend-layers.title: Ubersight trend layers
m-ubersight-trend-layers.speaker: Estelle Gohil, Fiftyfive5, Week 2 (Fiftyfive5's own tool)

beats.say: Ubersight trend layers work down from cultural drivers, to macro trends, to micro trends, and finally to the tension where the opportunity sits.
Take drinking. The driver is health. The macro trend is wellness. The micro trend is mocktails on a night out.
Here's the tension. People want to cut back, but still feel part of the party. A premium alcohol-free drink that looks the part resolves it.
Use it like this: trace a trend down the layers, then build your idea on the tension.

m-volatility-moat.title: The volatility moat: equity, reputation and crisis response
m-volatility-moat.speaker: Justin Papps, Tenet, Week 3

beats.say: The volatility moat. Strong brands survive turbulence when brand equity, reputation and crisis response all work together.
KFC in the UK once ran out of chicken. Customers turned up to closed doors, and they were furious.
But the brand owned it with a cheeky apology, and kept its equity and reputation. Tesla broke all three legs. VW survived on equity alone.
Use it like this: test a brand on all three legs before a crisis hits, not after.

m-what-vs-why.title: What vs why (say is not do) and the qualitative toolkit
m-what-vs-why.speaker: Estelle Gohil, Fiftyfive5, Week 2

beats.say: What versus why. Behavioural data from sales and dashboards shows what happened. Qualitative research uncovers why, by talking, watching and following people over time.
A shopper says she wants something cheaper. Keep asking why, and the real driver turns out to be saving time.
Estelle's team put body cameras on baristas. Watching the footage surfaced carton problems nobody had mentioned when asked.
Use it like this: name the what the client already has, then pick two or three qualitative methods to find the why.

w10.title: Inside the world of influencer marketing
w10.speaker: Bryce Coombe

beats.say: Week ten. Inside the world of influencer marketing, with Bryce Coombe, managing director of Hypetap. His message: influencer is no longer a side channel.
Hypetap is a full service influencer agency, founded in twenty fourteen. It calls itself more than a platform, running on people, process and product.
Australia has twenty one point three million social media users, each on six or more platforms a month. And TikTok time is up six hours on last year.
Guess the average Australian TikTok user. She's a thirty nine year old woman, watching a movie's worth, about ninety minutes, every single night.
Why does it work? Eighty percent are on TikTok mainly for creators. Seventy five percent have acted on a product in their feed. And twenty percent use social for inspiration while buying.
But value is different here. A creator's recipe showing cookware in real life gets positive sentiment. Strict brand instructions get neutral sentiment at best.
Social is now search. Nearly half of US consumers use TikTok as a search engine. Google indexes creator content, and AI models learn about brands from it.

So it's not just another channel that interrupts the broadcast. It works through peer validation, algorithmic trust and cultural resonance, which beats standard attention by two hundred and forty six percent.
Know your brand's eye level. Leader brands use experts. Eye to eye brands use just like you creators. Subservient brands do the work for people.
Fast growth attracts opportunists. Brands that treat creators transactionally, influencers who fake their reach, and agency cowboys. His rule: never trust a screen grab.

The big one: the brand is liable, not the influencer. A free product counts as paid advertising, so it must be disclosed. Infringement notices for a listed company reach a hundred and thirty three thousand dollars.
Assets count too. Music, clips, even a reposted meme can breach copyright. Warner Music is suing Crumbl Cookies. Rights owners wait for many breaches, then sue big.
AIMCO's Code of Practice cuts legal risk and wasted spend, with clear rules for contracts and reporting. For consumers, it means choice, protection and trust.
Brand safety is deeper than a few thumb scrolls. Check deleted posts, fit, swearing and politics. Kmart's celebrity pair looked good on paper, but audiences said, these two don't shop at Kmart.
Finally, measure growth, not just attention. Views and engagement explain attention. Growth comes from visibility, mental availability, share of voice, brand perception and behaviour change.
Want in? Account management is a good entry point, because it covers everything. And bring something extra, or you're lost in a sea of sameness.
So treat influencer as a specialist discipline. Know the brand carries the legal risk. And measure growth, not just attention. That's week ten.

w11.title: Inside a media agency: strategy, automation and AI
w11.speaker: Ali Coysh and Geoff Clarke

beats.say: Week eleven goes inside a media agency. First, Ali Coysh, National Head of Strategy at Initiative, on how media strategy works.
Fifteen years ago, media, creative and PR agencies sat around the client. Now it's crowded with analytics and in-house teams too.
Four things drove that: more channels, the rise of specialists, economic pressure on budgets, and a data boom, along with privacy laws.
So who owns strategy? Creative and media agencies used to work together. Now they compete for it, both pitching to the same client.
Media's job has grown too. It used to be planning, buying and reporting on paid media. Now it orchestrates experiences across owned, earned, shared and paid.
To choose channels, strategists weigh eight inputs. Who's the audience, what do they watch, what's happening in culture, and where do they shop the category?
Then the hard numbers. Which channel works best? What does modelling say drives return? Which markets matter, and what creative assets are there?
Every decision follows one logic flow. Journey stage, then the bond or barrier, the media role, and then channel, platform and the exact environment.
Take Lego City. Kids felt it was losing out to newer, cooler toys. So Lego partnered with Nitro Circus and reignited the love.
Crown wasn't seen as a dining destination. So it sponsored MasterChef on TV, rebuilding its dining credentials where food lovers were watching.
In Queensland, locals saw NRMA as an outsider. So it teamed up with the Courier Mail on Help our highway, campaigning to fix the Bruce Highway.
It worked. NRMA hit its best non-customer consideration in Queensland in six years, and the government committed four hundred and sixty-seven million dollars.
Ali's answer to creative versus media? Creative and media. Insight, creativity, collaboration, and human thinking plus AI.

Then Geoff Clarke, Chief Operating Officer of IPG Mediabrands Australia. ChatGPT reached about seven hundred million users in under two years, so regulation, ethics and education are playing catch-up.

board.title: Bots, AI and **people**
board.name: Geoff Clarke
board.org: Chief Operating Officer, IPG Mediabrands Australia

beats.say: Here's the false economy. Upstream work is now heavily AI driven, but downstream, seventy percent of the workload, is still highly manual.
So agencies built bots. Trigger bots react to an email, automatic bots take over next, and schedule bots run at set times. Geoff calls them an invisible police force.
Bots now run TV setup, bookings and budget reconciliation. With offshoring, they saved about two hundred and seven thousand hours in five years, and clients became partners.
So what skills matter? Data-driven thinking, creative and strategic thinking, and adaptability. The lasting edge is the craft of your people.
So: media orchestrates experiences, choices follow the logic flow, and bots take the grind. Use AI to free time for high-value work, and lead the change. That's week eleven.
Week twelve: measuring what matters. Nicky Barton, Head of Marketing Science at Mutinex, on how marketers work out what actually works.
Mutinex helps brands find what drives sales. GrowthOS reads the market, Nicky's team translates, and brands decide where the next dollar goes.
London, 1854. Cholera spread through Soho and experts blamed bad air. But data on where the deaths happened pointed to the water.
Marketing had the same problem. For decades it ran on surveys, sales data months late, and the gut feel of the most senior person in the room.
Then tracking grew. Banner ads showed clicks, AdWords intent, analytics visits, Facebook and the iPhone who you are, and the pixel what you buy.
So last touch became the default: the last click gets all the credit. It's a group assignment where whoever hits submit gets the whole mark.
Picture this shopper. She saw a billboard, heard the radio, then clicked a search ad. The billboard gets zero credit, the search ad a hundred percent.
So budgets flow to the bottom of the funnel, brand looks useless, and mental availability shrinks. Nike went direct, pulled back from retail, and people stopped seeing it.
Then privacy broke tracking. Safari limits, GDPR, then Apple's ask app not to track pop-up. Meta estimated that one pop-up cost it ten billion dollars in a year.

board.title: One **pop-up**
board.caption: Meta's own estimate of **one year's** cost

beats.say: Ask every platform how much it sold and the answers add up to over a hundred percent. Everyone did the assignment.
Enter marketing mix modelling. Weekly sales, media spend, price, promotions, seasons, the economy and competitors go in. Out come what drove sales, ROI by channel and the next dollar.
It's probabilistic, not deterministic. Not this click caused this sale, but the most likely effect, and how sure we are. More honest, and privacy safe.
A cafe on a busy corner gets walk-ins with zero ads. That's baseline. And ads keep working after they stop, like a song stuck in your head.
Add the fifth slice of pizza: returns diminish. Last year's star channel may not be the next best bet. And test first, like a flight simulator.

Across eighty-three brands in Australia and New Zealand, many drifted to performance. Those keeping brand muscle grew most. Yet cinema, radio and free-to-air, the longest lasting channels, were cut first.
If you can't add budget, don't add channels. Spreading money thinner shrinks results, and brands that go off air pay later.
Measurement has moved from the marketing report to the boardroom. The CEO asks what revenue and profit this created, and the CFO trusts the budget.
The numbers get easier to produce, so judgement becomes the job. The best marketers bring curiosity, comfort with numbers, commercial sense and storytelling.
So: last touch misleads, privacy broke tracking, and modelling reads the whole market. Keep your brand muscle, and always ask, how do we know it worked? That's week twelve.
Week thirteen is different. No guest speaker, just a Q and A with the unit coordinator about the final exam, plus Teresa's email to the class.
It's Monday the twenty-third of November at one pm. Venues vary, so check your own timetable, and find the personal email from the exams office. Look in junk too.
Bring your own device. Your phone gets you the start passcode, then goes to the front desk. Your laptop needs Respondus lockdown software installed beforehand.
Before the day, try the practice test on the exam site so the form isn't new to you. And only a pre-approved dictionary is allowed.
The format is five short essay or scenario questions, six marks each, thirty marks in total. Answer every part, a, b and so on.
Aim for about three to four hundred words an answer, and five hundred at most. There's no formal minimum, so keep it to the point.
What's tested? The concepts, models and ideas from the guest lectures and the workshop recaps. Where a speaker named a model, expect a question on it.
What's not tested? Speakers' career paths, exact dates, and full media plans. Background on a company will mostly be given to you in the question.
Each question sticks to one lecture. Speakers wrote questions on their own talk, so learn each lecture's own concepts, even where themes overlap.
Job roles aren't a framework to learn. But a question could describe a company problem and ask who would be involved, and what process they'd follow.
The big skill is transfer. A concept a speaker showed with Telstra might be asked about Qantas. Know the concept, not just the example.
Watch the wording. Why did X do this wants the speaker's reasoning. Could Y do it too wants your own justified view.
There's no universal marking formula and no fixed one mark per element. Follow the exact task and every subpart, and be precise. A formal essay structure isn't needed.
So for each answer: name and explain the concept, apply it step by step to the brand in the question, then link it to the outcome. An opinion alone won't cut it.
To revise, go back through every lecture's notes, the workshop and tutorial questions, and the pre-work. Focus on the lectures, not your report or presentation.
And don't bother asking your tutor what's in the exam. Tutors genuinely don't know the questions.
On the day, have Respondus installed and tested, your laptop charged with the charger packed, your phone for the passcode, and your venue checked. Arrive early.
So: five questions, six marks each, one lecture per question. Know each concept well enough to use it on a brand the speaker never mentioned. Good luck. That's week thirteen.
Week two. Market research and consumer insights, with Estelle Gohil from Fifty-five Five. Her job is to take complexity and make it simple enough to decide on.
Behavioural data tells you what happened, like people drinking less. It can't tell you why, and the why decides what the business does.
A shopper says, I want something cheaper. But the real driver might be value for money or saving time. So keep asking why.
Meanwhile the dashboards pile up, CRM and sales data. But too much data creates complexity, not simplicity, and none of it makes a decision on its own.
Research drives growth three ways. Identify where to play. Execute how to win, from the value proposition to pricing. And evaluate what matters.
Why not just add gen AI? It can't close three gaps: cultural understanding, data that doesn't exist yet, and the analysis itself. Keep a human in the lead.

lines.text: Human **in the lead**, in the loop

beats.say: The toolkit starts with talking. Discussion groups of six to ten. Conflict encounters, putting Apple fans with Samsung fans. And consumer juries that deliver a verdict.
Cognitive interviewing uses memory to reach emotion. What made you hesitate? In mobile ethnography, people film their own lives on their phones, in the moment.
Then there's watching. On a shopping safari you follow someone. What do they pick up, then put back? What people say isn't what they do.
Consumer immersions put the client on a bus into a lower socio-economic neighbourhood. Not to interview the consumer, but to briefly become them.
Longer methods include agile innovation loops, digital communities and case studies from many angles. Social listening is where AI genuinely helps.
One project put body cameras on baristas. At speed, they weren't thinking about plant milk cartons. Watching the footage back surfaced opening, storage and disposal problems.
A tea brand ran seven markets together to find the similarities, not make separate campaigns. And an ad built on jokes is hard to land across seven cultures.
For universities, demand and performance data make two maps. Existing programs plot performance against attractiveness, new ones momentum against size. But numbers can't explain why students choose.
Their tool Ubersight layers cultural drivers, macro trends, micro trends and tension. Dynamic personas use the client's own data, so you can question a segment.
AI does help. It scans every transcript, and one real consumer clip beats a slide deck. But it makes mistakes, and words miss tone and body language.
Her lingering worry is the Emperor's New Clothes: everyone agrees the output is good when it may not be. Watch for bias, in the tool and in yourself.
So understand people, don't just collect data. Keep asking why. Insight must enable a decision, and AI is a tool, not a replacement. That's week two.

lines.text: AI is a **tool**, not a replacement

w3.title: What are brands and why do they matter?
w3.speaker: Justin Papps

beats.say: Week three. Why do brands matter? Justin Papps from Tenet defines a brand as beliefs and perceptions that create a positive predisposition at the point of choice.

board.title: What are **brands** and why do they matter?
board.name: Justin Papps

beats.say: So a brand lives in the customer's head, not your guidelines, and the work happens before purchase. Marketing is persuasion.
Brand first meant to burn. Then the mark showed ownership, then who made it, then a reputation for quality. Now it means what it says about you.
Associations cluster around the founder, what the company does, and adjectives. Tesla shows the founder link cuts both ways. Keep the link positive and consistent.
Brand exposures went from ten to twenty a day in the seventeen hundreds to ten thousand today, and our brains haven't grown. The battle moved from the aisle to a phone screen.
Five reasons brands matter: economic engines, behavioural shortcuts, strategy in action, shaping culture, and volatility moats.
One, economic engines. A Louis Vuitton backpack costs fifteen point six times a Maverick and Co bag that beats it on compartments and warranty.
An iPhone costs about four hundred and fifty to make and sells for up to sixteen hundred, a margin of sixty-seven percent plus. If brands didn't matter, Amazon would list products alphabetically.
Two, behavioural shortcuts. Kahneman's System One is about ninety-five percent of thinking: fast and unconscious. System Two is slow and logical, for big decisions. Brands aim at System One.
Brand strategy rests on four pillars: relevance, distinctiveness, consistency and availability. Land all four and you get cut-through and salience.
Distinctive assets compound with age. But Ipsos found a paradox: logos are in ninety-four percent of ads and return one point four times. Sonic cues are in six percent and return eight point five.
Three, strategy in action. Segmentation, targeting and positioning are business decisions with trade-offs. Get them right for a positive return on marketing investment.
Four, brands shape culture. Harley-Davidson, Nike's Kaepernick ad and the RTA speeding campaign work. Pepsi's Kendall Jenner ad failed, borrowing a movement it had no standing in.
Five, volatility moats: equity, reputation and crisis response. Tesla broke all three. Volkswagen survived Dieselgate on equity alone. KFC's FCK bucket rebuilt equity.
Consumer equity grows most through referral from family and friends. Stop advertising and you fade from memory, and getting back costs more than holding on.
An unknown laptop brand can have the best specs and still no trust. Brands must be machine readable and human loveable, not AI slop.
Marketing is a long game, often two to three years. Sampling breaks the uncertainty barrier. And in B2B, lean on the rational case and keep clear promises.
So win before the point of choice, and audit your assets. Attention is cheap. Memory is expensive. Preference is priceless. That's week three.

w4.title: Managing brands with creativity and humanity
w4.speaker: Brent Smart

beats.say: Week four, with Brent Smart, former CMO of Telstra and IAG. Marketing is a battle for memory, and the biggest risk is taking no risk.

board.title: Managing brands with **creativity and humanity**
board.name: Brent Smart
board.org: Founder, B.Smart; formerly CMO of Telstra and IAG

beats.say: You're competing with how people spend their time. And categories look identical: bottled water is always an alpine stream.
Liquid Death broke every code and became the fastest-growing water brand in the world. Great ideas often sound stupid at first. That's the signal.
Creative work returns two and a half times the revenue growth and four times the profit of the average ad. Dull costs twenty and a half million extra.
He's proved it three times. Yellow Pages' treehouse used zero paid media. Cheerios rode out a backlash. NRMA's koalas went from thirty-sixth to fifth.
If it's not bold, it's dumb. Bad ideas are safe and comfortable. Good ones feel uncomfortable, and with no data, conviction does the work.
Telstra's reputation sat barely above the tax office. Asked to draw the brand, people drew a suit, the Monopoly man, a bully.
Only fifteen percent of buyers are in market now, ready for logic and offers. The other eighty-five percent need emotion, memories for later.
Don't just talk to the four hands that are up right now. Someone buying a phone in three years is worth reaching today.
Activation spikes, then drops when you stop. Brand building rises slowly. The benchmark is sixty percent brand. Telstra was at twenty, so he went to fifty first.
Be a magnet, not a mirror. Put a still from your ad, logo removed, beside three rivals. If nobody can tell which is yours, it's a mirror.
Telstra made twenty-six stop-motion ads, each an Australian animal in a real place, with forty-two local voices and handmade puppets. It won a Grand Prix.
The brand on one page: a connected future for everyone. Positioning, engineering possibility. The platform, wherever we go. Always crafted with a human hand.
The whistling ad used animation, no phones and metaphor. At launch, people hated it. But being noticed beats being liked, so he held his nerve.
Then people started copying the walk. Thirty million organic TikTok views, zero paid spend, and Telstra credited the people who made them.
Even the posters were handmade. People can tell made from generated, and read effort as care. Craft is a strategic choice.
Marketing ROI rose from six point one to ten point four in four years, on lower spend. Even performance marketing converted better, thanks to a stronger brand.
With AI, content is either slop or irreplaceably human. Telstra's AI Santa took eight hundred thousand calls. But you need an idea first.
So make the brand memorable, build future demand, and craft it with a human hand. Creativity thrives on kindness, so be kind. That's week four.
Week five. Managing the evolution of brands, with Shannon Wright, Head of Marketing for Confectionery at Nestlé Oceania. She leads KitKat and Allen's.

board.title: Managing the **evolution** of brands
board.name: Shannon Wright
board.org: Head of Marketing, Confectionery, Nestlé Oceania

beats.say: First, career advice. Be interested in the unfamiliar, know what matters to you, stay curious, and be a good person. The industry is small.
Two brands, opposite problems. KitKat takes the consistency path. Allen's must define its long-term path as trends shift underneath it.
KitKat stands for a break. It was made for workers on their break, and the bar takes two hands to snap, so you stop.
Three truths line up. Brand belief: breaks are good. Audience truth: everyone needs one. Product truth: it's made to be broken.
The most dangerous person in marketing is the bored brand manager, who changes things that didn't need changing. Have a strategy.
Consistency is a superpower. The need hasn't changed, but the tension has. Sixty three percent of Gen Z need a break, yet sixty four percent can't switch off.
They sit down, doom scroll, and their minds stay busy. So KitKat's job now is the emotional break, not just the physical one.
Distinctive brand assets shortcut people to you: the bar, the red, the snap. Use them or lose them. Even Have a, unfinished, works, because your brain closes the gap.
The second most dangerous person is the brand manager with no ambition. Cultural relevance is a currency. Impact comes from brand size, creative quality and budget setting.
Fans argued over the right way to eat a KitKat: around twenty seven million social engagements. A debate about your brand is a jackpot, so fan the flames.
Four principles. Meet your audience where they are. Tone and timing are everything. Be clear on the brand's role. And subvert your equity to be one of the people.
Now Allen's. People love it, but a brand is a leaky bucket that drains unless you refill it. We want a playground, not a museum.
Gen Z want intense flavours and surprising textures. Forty five percent of Australians say texture appeals, and lolly salads turn sweets into social currency.
GLP-1 drugs could reach fifteen percent of Australians by year end, dulling the joy of sweets. And India has overtaken England for migration, bringing new tastes.
When Arnott's changed four Shapes flavours, people were outraged. A heritage brand doesn't have to taste better. It has to taste the same.
Know your consumers, potential consumers and brand. Then test any stretch for fit, distance from the core, consumer permission, risk versus reward, and keep monitoring.
For Heinz, soup is a near step, pasta sauce a credible stretch, vodka the exception. Or collaborate, like Allen's with Pepsi and Mountain Dew.
So: protect your assets, and know why you're entering culture. Know your consumers and who you are. Use AI to ease the work, not do the thinking. That's week five.

w6.title: Managing a brand for social purpose
w6.speaker: Libby Hogson

beats.say: Week six. Managing a brand for social purpose, with Libby Hogson from UNICEF Australia. Her premise: brand building in a charity is just brand building.

board.title: Managing a brand for **social purpose**
board.name: Libby Hogson
board.org: Director of Growth and Engagement, UNICEF Australia

beats.say: Over sixty thousand charities, one per four hundred and thirty nine Australians. Funding grows about three percent a year, but donors are falling. Fewer people, giving more.
Then trust. The Edelman Trust Barometer found sixty one percent of Australians hold grievances against institutions and the rich. Forty percent see hostile activism as legitimate.
When people feel an institution isn't serving them, trust falls. Trust tracks brand performance, so the trust problem is the growth problem.
Awareness was fuzzy too. Forty percent didn't know who UNICEF was, only twenty nine percent linked it to children, and many didn't know it was a charity.
About ninety five percent of spend went on conversion and retention, and only five percent on awareness. They were optimising a funnel with an empty top.
By 2020, UNICEF had zero unprompted awareness. Asked to name a charity, people never said it. Shown the name, they recognised it.
That gap matters. People with UNICEF top of mind showed nineteen percent donation intent. Aware only when prompted, just seven percent. Mental availability nearly triples intent.
So which facts to lead with? Saves more lives than any other organisation. The world's largest organisation for children's rights. Brings lifesaving help to children.
Then came a polycrisis: bushfires, the pandemic, Ukraine, all at once. UNICEF USA's version was too chest-beating for Australia. Positioning has to fit the moment.
The positioning: UNICEF inspires Australians with the determination it takes to protect and care for every child, no matter what. Determination is the key word.
The proof: on the ground in over a hundred and ninety countries, help within forty eight hours, and one hundred percent donor funded. The message: Always there.
Consistency isn't how you look. It's the place you hold in people's minds: one message, again and again, until you're sick of it and the public remembers.

Earned media was key, with ambassadors matched to the moment. From 2020 to 2024, broadcast share of voice rose from twenty to fifty five percent, and news mentions rose two hundred and seventy percent.
It was a whole of organisation job. The team moved from generalists to experts, and scrapped the digital marketing team so everyone could do digital.
Did it work? Ad awareness and share of voice lift unprompted awareness, then donation intent, then market share. Top of mind tracked alongside revenue growth.
After 2024 metrics dipped, but there's no tired brand, just a bored brand manager. Always there became Let's be there. And climate change fits, because it's changing childhood.
The lessons: it's a whole of organisation task, stay the course, measure everything, skilled people matter, and trust the data but still take risks. That's week six.
Week seven. Strategy in a creative agency, with Tim Collier, National Head of Strategy at Cummins and Partners. His advice: be curious, and be opinionated.

board.title: Strategy in a **creative agency**
board.name: Tim Collier
board.org: National Head of Strategy, Cummins & Partners

beats.say: A planner informs what the work says, and why it will work. The client brings a business problem, creatives bring the idea, and strategy sits between, speaking for the audience.

steps.text: **Strategy** how does it affect the audience?

beats.say: Planning was born in 1974, in Stephen King's Planning Guide at JWT London. A method must stimulate imagination, not just control it: realistic, pragmatic, fundamental and structured.
Planning has since split into three jobs. Brand planners own what's said and why. Comms planners own where, when and in what order. Media planners own who sees it.
Brand planning is the underlying message. Not just do it, but I can be an athlete if I just try.
The job is reading, research, writing, consulting and leading. Writing is the real skill: one page that inspires the creatives.
Tim wanted to design for General Pants, but did marketing work experience there. The people he met that week got him a decade of jobs. People who get jobs know people.
On social, stop thinking like a user. Media is cheap, so use scale. Don't blend in with the algorithm; stand out. Don't scam it either, it's a black box.
A strategist works in four steps: discover, synthesis, plan and instruct. The client hands you a five page brief with everything under the sun. Your first job is subtraction.
To discover, use the five Cs: company, culture, category, connections and consumer. Mostly desk research.
Bill Bernbach said nothing is so powerful as an insight into human nature. So watch people, and enjoy how strange they are. Frameworks add discipline, not the insight.
The basic brief is get, who, to, by. Get inspiring athletes, who just did this, to repurchase, by reminding them of something.
The single minded proposition is the hardest part. It's an invitation, not a claim. Not our chocolate is the richest, but what the richest chocolate tastes like, and this is ours.
To write a brief: gather everything, write the task plainly, get to a point of view, then rewrite and recap. Without a point of view, it's just a summary.
Then the planning cycle: where are we, why are we there, where could we be, how could we get there, and are we getting there? Then round again.
The Effie is the strategist's award, the only one that matters to Tim. It takes a four thousand word essay proving the campaign worked, because strategy leads to profit.
And we owe our clients. If an agency does a bad job, it probably won't get fired. The people in the factory will.
So learn, process, apply. Nobody reads advertising; people read what interests them, and sometimes it's an ad. Be curious and opinionated. That's week seven.
Week eight. Creating advertising that works, with Andrew Baxter, chair of Australian Pork, after twenty six years in agencies. His opener? Advertising is like selling fresh air.
He ran Ogilvy and Publicis. His advice: pick your side. Agency life jumps around, marketing management goes deep, and consulting sits in between.
Ad vertere is Latin for turn the mind toward. Posters go back to Pompeii. Since then, the town crier, newspapers, radio, TV, the internet and social.
Go where the eyeballs are. It used to be TV. Now it's the phone. And today it's about eighty percent science, twenty percent art.
Ads in Australia must be truthful. Fines run past a million dollars, so bring the receipts. Oddly, politics is exempt, because a court ruled there must be a financial outcome.
Daniel Kahneman showed about ninety five percent of purchases are intuitive. We buy first, then post rationalise, and rational ads mostly help us do that.
The Effie awards link ads to sales. But success can backfire. Lamb ads worked so well that people think lamb is only for Australia Day.
Advertising is simple: right message, right person, right place, right time. KFC and McDonald's switch screens by the hour, tradies at three, families at six.
Making an ad takes four steps. Strategy, the idea, making it, which doesn't always work out, and placing it. Strategy is just ten percent of an agency, yet everyone wants in.
You get fifteen words or less. A billboard gets a two second glance. And use one message per ad, like powerful wash in cold water. Don't get too clever.
Ads move people down a funnel: awareness, liking, preference, conviction, purchase. Aim to reach about sixty five percent of your audience at least three times.
Kraft Easy Mac sold to mums, for teenage boys who get home hungry. The message: fills them up, fast to make. Kill hunger fast became the hunger blaster when the client balked.
The most effective ads are famous, with seventy two percent outselling rivals. Emotional, successful sixty two percent of the time. And single minded and memorable.
Differentiation matters most. While Christmas ads all looked alike, John Lewis made Monty the Penguin, pure emotion. A hundred and thirty two million pounds in extra sales, and eight to one ROI.
AI now helps with research, synthetic audiences, and many versions of content to test. Nine in ten marketing teams already use it.
Marketing mix models show which channels worked together. Winning campaigns average ten point two. Digital now takes about sixty percent of media spend, led by Google, Meta and Amazon.
John Singleton said advertising exists to sell. Mostly, but sometimes it's to change behaviour. So keep it simple, emotional and single minded. Make famous work that works. That's week eight.

w9.title: Creativity: the last remaining commercial superpower
w9.speaker: Brendan Willenberg

beats.say: Week nine. Creativity, the last remaining commercial superpower, with Brendan Willenberg, an executive creative director. As automation flattens everything, creativity is what sets a company apart.
His big claim: commercial creativity is cheating. Same inputs as everyone, but an unfair advantage. Good creative thinking is distinct, simple, unexpected and obvious, often by trimming things away.
He learned from Edward de Bono's lateral thinking. Vertical thinking plays with the pieces you have. Lateral thinking changes the pieces, redefining the problem so a whole new solution is possible.

Creativity is fancy problem solving, so first find the real problem. It's usually buried beneath what you're told. So go from the brief, past the expected response, to the real problem, and the solution.
Rexona wanted to own summer and sport on a small budget, but sponsorship is cluttered and expensive. If you can't buy media, earn it. Pitvertising had fans guessing where the Rexona was hiding.
The lesson: creativity thrives on constraint. Blue sky thinking rarely works. If the problem is wide open, tighten it yourself.
Extra gum sales were falling, because at the checkout people are on their phones. So the Bad Breath Index suggested gum as strong food was scanned. A new idea in a familiar context.
Kia's hybrids had nothing different to say. So they said nothing in the most interesting way possible. Lean into the uncomfortable truth, with the solution in your pocket.
V Energy can't out Red Bull Red Bull. So instead of copying, it called bull on the whole category. Say one thing over and over, until it becomes your distinction.
There are three types of agency: media, creative and integrated. All of them overcomplicate things, partly to look smart. The real intelligence is untangling it back to a single line.
The creative method runs from the brief, problem and strategy, through creative territories and the brand platform, to roll out, production and optimisation. It's stressful. You fret in the unknown.
Creative people aren't special. They're just comfortable in the unknown. An idea is a new combination of existing things. Gum plus a scanner. A logo plus an armpit.
Gather insights and lots of what ifs. Be okay with bad ideas, and cross them out. When you run out of bad ideas, you take a leap.
So be a better client. Brief the problem, not what you want to say. Punters don't think like you do. Be simple, not just smart. It's not creative if it's not commercial.
And AI? It can speed run the process. No ego, never tired. But alone it gives similar, cheap ideas. Use it as your antagonist, not your assistant.
Getting in? Bring an open heart and a curious mind. Find the real problem, embrace constraint, and say one thing well. Creativity is still the superpower. That's week nine.
